newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait finalising British missile deal-sources.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait finalising British missile deal-sources.

text.p: Kuwait is finalising a deal with Britain for Sea Skua missiles despite a demand by the Gulf Arab state's parliament to further probe the contract, industry experts said on Sunday.
"The final details are being worked out now and some of the (related) documents were recently intialed," said an executive familiar with the programme.

Political sources said parliament had not been officially notified that the government had started to implement a decision to buy the British Aerospace Plc surface-to-surface missiles, which were successfully used in the 1991 Gulf War.
"If it is true, this is a disaster," said a leading MP, predicting a clash with the government over the deal for ignoring the demand for a fresh debate.

Parliament was due to discuss the deal last Tuesday but postponed the debate until Defence Minister Sheikh Salem Sabah al-Salem al-Sabah returns from London. He flew to Britain earlier this month with Prime Minister and Crown Prince Sheikh Saad al-Abdulla al-Sabah who is receiving medical treatment.
A Western industry expert said:"The first stage of the (Sea Skua) deal has been completed ... follow up steps are underway."

Kuwait newspapers earlier said the deal was for around $90 million but experts said the contract was split into several deals, including training and a British gift of 20 Sea Skua missiles, making it difficult to give an exact figure.
"But I do not think it is worth $90 million, a little bit less than that," said one expert.
The previous parliament in 1996 asked its Public Funds Protection Committee to probe the deal after a cheaper offer for France's Aerospatiale MM-15 missile was dropped.
The missiles will arm Kuwait's eight, French-made fast patrol boats ordered in 1995. The first of the 42-metre vessels was completed last month.
Parliamentary sources said the ministries of defence and finance had sufficient funds allocated for arms purchases to complete the deal without having to return to parliament.

"They can go ahead without (consulting) us and use executive powers," said a disappointed MP. "People ask us 'why are you making such a fuss about a small deal?' But that is not the point, it is a matter of principle."
Diplomats said MPs might form a protest committee to discuss the issue with Kuwaiti leaders.

Sheikh Salem said last month in a written response to an MP's question that the British offer included a pledge by London to settle a seven million pound ($11 million) debt. Days later, 16 MPs responded with a motion demanding a full parliament debate of the deal and a smaller pending one for Chinese mortars.
